choices.why: Standard rendering of ἐξουσία in contexts of delegated power, especially over spirits; alternatives like 'power' or 'right' are less precise for apostolic commission.
Present imperative plural matching the apostolic command; alternatives like 'cure' or 'treat' lack the specific connotation of restoring wholeness implied in charismatic healing.
Accusative plural of νεκρός as direct object of ἐγείρετε; 'dead ones' is grammatically possible but wooden in English; 'the dead' is idiomatic for the group.
Accusative plural of λεπρός; 'leprous ones' is literally accurate but archaic in English; 'lepers' is the established term for those afflicted with leprosy in biblical contexts.
Accusative plural of δαίμων; while 'evil spirits' is a possible gloss, the text contrasts these with πνεύματα elsewhere, and 'demons' is the specific term used in exorcism contexts.
Adverbial use of δωρεάν; 'gratuitously' or 'without cost' are possible but less natural in the imperative; 'freely' captures the grace-and-mission tone of Matthew 10:8.

Anarthrous but clearly referring to the Holy Spirit in this context of charismatic operations; 'a spirit' would be theologico-logically incoherent here; capitalized per convention for divine reference.

Charisma in Pauline usage denotes grace-given capacities; 'graces' is possible but less common in English theological usage; 'spiritual gifts' adds clarity but the context already establishes pneumatology.

Adverb from οἰκονομία; here meaning 'by divine dispensation' or 'as part of God's plan'; 'stewardly' or ' administratively' are too vague; 'economically' in the older sense of 'household management' fits the theological usage.
Genitive dependent on τάξη; 'of a sign' is literal; 'miraculous' adds interpretation not in the genitive; 'token' is possible but 'sign' is standard in Pauline rhetoric for miraculous attestation.
Dative plural of πιστός; 'believers' is a possible synonym but 'faithful' carries the covenant nuance of trustworthiness in response to God, fitting the context of signs for conviction.
Accusative of διανομή; 'giving' or 'bestowal' are close but 'distribution' better captures the Spirit's active, varied apportioning implied by διαφόρως ἐν ἑκάστῳ.
παχὺ means thick or substantial, δὴ adds emphasis, τοῦτο refers to the earthly body previously mentioned; together they denote the tangible, physical human body as opposed to spiritual

choices.english: through the vast multitude of holy ones
choices.why: διὰ + genitive expresses agency; πολλῆς modifies ἁγίων πληθύος, emphasizing the large number of sanctified individuals forming the Church; 'vast' conveys the quantitative sense better than 'much'

τελεωτάτην is the superlative of τελεώτατος, meaning 'brought to completion' or 'most perfect'; in theological context, it refers to the Church's ultimate unity in divine understanding, so 'most complete' captures both the grammatical superlative and the theological sense

περιπεποικιλμένῳ is a perfect passive participle of περιποικίλλυμι, meaning 'varied all around' or 'diversified'; in context of ἱματισμῷ διαχρύσῳ (golden garment), it describes the richly diverse spiritual gifts adorning the Church; 'variegated' is the standard theological rendering for this term in patristic Greek

choices.term: γλώσσῃ 290 τε ἁπάσῃ καὶ ἔθνει παντὶ
choices.english: by tongue 290, and to every people
choices.why: γλώσσῃ is dative of instrument; 290 is a numeral (likely referring to a specific linguistic group or symbolic number); τε connects it to the following phrase; ἁπάσῃ modifies γλώσσῃ, ἔθνει παντὶ is dative of indirect object; the phrase indicates the apostles were enabled to speak in 290 languages to all nations
rejected: by the 290th tongue and every nation

pass_b_english: He granted the holy apostles authority over unclean spirits, so that they could cast them out.
Indeed, he told them: 'Heal the sick, raise the dead, cleanse those with leprosy, cast out demons. You received freely—so give freely.'
Moreover, he certainly said, 'Heal the sick, raise the dead, cleanse the lepers, cast out demons; freely you received, freely give.'
Moreover, the mighty works of divine power are not scattered apart but flow from the one Spirit.
Consider how Moses cast his staff to the ground and it became a serpent, how he turned the rivers to blood, how he drew water from the rock.
The blessed prophets have accomplished nearly all that surpasses mere word and wonder—yet we affirm that these mighty operations proceed from the one Spirit.
Still, someone may prophesy, but never apart from the Spirit.
Another may discern spirits, but only within that same Spirit.
As for what kinds of spirits are involved, we have spoken of this before.

One person confidently assures others that he knows various kinds of tongues, and also claims to interpret them—yet this gift we regard as particular, bestowed by divine economy according to need and opportunity.
Some indeed spoke in tongues though they had never learned them; others understood by interpreting, although long ago such practices were unfamiliar to the ear and not customary among such people.
Thus the divine Paul has been given to those who now insist on speaking in tongues—not as a mere share of grace, but as a sign-gift ordered for the faithful.
He also set forth this prophetic word: 'I will speak to this people in foreign tongues and with other lips, yet even so they will not believe.' (Isaiah 66:18)
And the Spirit works differently in each person as he distributes the gifts.

For just as this substantial body, formed from the earth, is composed of many parts, so too Christ’s body—that is, the Church—is constituted through the vast multitude of the holy into the most complete unity of intelligent understanding.
In this, the blessed David also says he has surrounded her with a golden garment, variegated, which I take to signify the manifold and precious charismata.
Thus, those who were to be initiators under the sun were about to speak in tongue 290 and to every nation the evident and saving proclamation of the gospel; for this purpose, he gave them tongues.
They were men of Galilee, trained according to Judea, Hebrews and from Hebrews, Medes and Parthians, and moreover Elamites—sixteen.
